creative.body:
I opened my chart at 6 in the morning and saw "estradiol: undetectable."

That was the day I understood my oncologist had no plan for the part of survivorship nobody talks about.

I am 61. I had stage one HR-positive breast cancer in March of 2022. Lumpectomy in April. 21 rounds of radiation in May and June.

And then, the day after my last radiation appointment, my oncologist handed me a small white slip of paper with one word on it.

Letrozole. A pill I would take every morning for the next 5 years to make sure the cancer didn't come back.

The first month was fine. The second month was fine. By the fourth month I started waking up at 3 in the morning soaked through my nightgown. By the sixth month my hair was thinner. By the eighth month I noticed that sex hurt in a way it had never hurt before.

Not soreness. Not friction.

A burning that started 2 seconds after my husband touched me and lasted for an hour after we stopped trying.

I told my oncologist at my 6-month visit. She nodded the way doctors nod when they have heard the same complaint 40 times that month and have nothing useful to offer. She said the words I now know every woman on an aromatase inhibitor hears at her 6-month visit.

Try Replens. Try a lubricant. Try coconut oil.

I tried all of them. None of them worked.

At my next visit, the PA opened my chart, scrolled, and offered me 2 things. A referral to pelvic floor physical therapy. Or a stronger prescription moisturizer she could send to the pharmacy that afternoon.

I sat in the chair in my paper gown and I told her I would think about it.

I did not schedule the PT. I did not call the pharmacy on the drive home. I went home, took off my coat, made coffee, and sat down at the kitchen table.

Then I opened MyChart on my laptop, the same way I used to open patient charts when I worked in administration, and I started reading.

Not the lab values. The guidelines. The full ones, the ones with citations.

I had spent 30 years watching clinicians read these documents on the job, and it had not occurred to me until that morning that I was now the patient in the chart, and nobody else was going to read the guideline for me.

A year in, I logged into my MyChart at 6 in the morning because I could not sleep. My latest labs were posted. Estradiol: undetectable.

I stared at that number for a long time.

Estradiol is the form of estrogen that keeps a woman's body soft. It keeps the vaginal walls thick. It keeps the bacteria balanced. It keeps the tissue alive.

Mine had been driven to 0 on purpose, by the medication I was taking on purpose, to stop a cancer that had been driven by it.

I am not angry at my oncologist. She saved my life. The letrozole is doing what it is supposed to do.

But the protocol for what they call genitourinary syndrome of menopause, when it happens to a cancer survivor on an aromatase inhibitor, is not a real protocol. It is a list of 3 things every oncologist's physician assistant says in a tired voice, in a fluorescent office, after the real medical conversation is over.

Try Replens. Try lube. Try coconut oil. Come back in 6 months.

I want to name what that is, because I sat with it for a long time before I had a word for it.

That is the polite version of the standard of care.

It is what they say when they have 90 seconds and a waiting room full of women. The actual standard, the one written down in the literature she trained on, is something else entirely.

The polite version is not a lie. It is a triage. It is not the same thing as evidence-based first-line care, and I had been treating it as if it were.

I am a retired hospital administrator. I know how to read a chart. I know how to read a guideline.

So I started reading.

The American Society of Clinical Oncology published a guideline in 2018. It is called Interventions to Address Sexual Problems in People With Cancer.

The summary recommendation, in plain language, is this.

Non-hormonal vaginal moisturizers used regularly are the first-line therapy for survivors with vaginal symptoms. Lubricants for use during sex are second-line. Pelvic floor physical therapy is recommended. Low-dose vaginal estrogen is permitted only with multidisciplinary input, meaning your oncologist has to sign off, and many will not.

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network survivorship guideline says the same thing. The North American Menopause Society says the same thing.

3 of the most authoritative bodies in oncology and women's health, all in agreement, all pointing at the same first-line treatment.

A non-hormonal vaginal moisturizer.

Then I started reading what was actually in the products my oncologist's PA had recommended.

Replens is a polycarbophil gel. It coats the vaginal wall and slowly releases water. It does one thing. It hydrates the surface. That is the entire mechanism.

Coconut oil is a saturated fat. It sits on top of the tissue. It does not get absorbed in any meaningful way. It also disrupts the vaginal microbiome by feeding the wrong bacteria.

Lubricants are lubricants. They are designed for the moment of friction. They are not designed for the tissue.

There is a number I came across in the literature that I have not been able to stop thinking about.

70 to 93% of women on aromatase inhibitors develop GSM symptoms. Of those, fewer than 5% are offered any treatment that meets the modern guideline definition.

I read that twice.

Almost every woman on the medication I was on was going to feel what I was feeling. And almost none of us were going to be offered the actual standard.

Here is the thing I had to understand before any of the rest of it made sense.

The postmenopausal vagina, on an aromatase inhibitor, is not just dry. The dryness is the symptom you feel.

There are 4 things going wrong underneath it.

The deep tissue is dehydrated. The lactobacillus colonies that used to keep the environment acidic and protected have collapsed. The glycogen that those bacteria fed on, the substrate the vaginal epithelium used to make when estrogen was around, is no longer being produced. And whatever you do put in to help the situation, if it is a one-shot product, is gone again within hours.

So when I lined up the products my oncology office had recommended against the 4 things the tissue actually needs, the math was brutal.

Replens hydrates the surface. That is one of 4.

Coconut oil sits on top of the tissue and feeds the wrong bacteria. That is 0 of 4, and arguably negative one.

Lubricants are designed for the 20 minutes of friction and then they are gone. That is also 0 of 4.

I had been told for almost 2 years that the non-hormonal answer was already on the shelf.

It wasn't.

Around this time I called a friend who had retired from nursing 3 years before me. She gave me the name of an oncology nurse navigator at the hospital where she had worked. We talked on the phone for 40 minutes.

She told me she sees 4 women a week with the exact symptoms I had. The PAs send them home with the same 3-product list I had been given. She said she had stopped tracking which prescriber sent them, because the answer was always the same, and the chart never had a slot for what happened next.

She told me the women who do well are the ones who go home and read for themselves.

That sentence stayed with me for the rest of the week.

What the guidelines, when you read them carefully, are pointing toward is 4 things at once.

Hydration of the deep tissue, not just the surface. Restoration of the lactobacillus bacteria that keep the vaginal environment healthy and acidic. Substrate for those bacteria to actually colonize and thrive on. Glycogen, which your body's own estrogen used to provide and which the aromatase inhibitor has now suppressed. And a sustaining prebiotic that keeps the work going between doses.

I started looking for a product that did all 4.

There was not one. Not in any drug store. Not on Amazon. Not on the shelves of my local pharmacy.

I want to stop here for a second, because this is where a lot of women like me get stuck.

Once you know estrogen is off the table, you start being told "natural" is the safe direction. Phytoestrogens. DHEA. Wild yam. Sea buckthorn.

The implication is that anything plant-derived is automatically safer than the pharmaceutical you are already taking.

That is not how this works.

The whole point of an aromatase inhibitor is to drive estrogenic activity to 0. A plant molecule that mimics estrogen at the receptor, even weakly, is exactly the thing the medication is trying to prevent.

"Natural" is not a category an oncologist cares about. The receptor is.

Phytoestrogen, DHEA, hormone analog, anything that converts to a hormone in the body, all of it sits on the no-list whether it grew in a field or came out of a lab.

So I made my own no-list and I started reading ingredient panels the way I used to read lab values.

Anything with a phytoestrogen, no. Anything with DHEA, no. Anything with a hormone or a hormone analog, no. Parabens, no. Phthalates, no.

That is when I found a small company called Avelle.

I found them through a clinical trial registry, of all places. Not an ad. Not a recommendation from my oncologist.

Avelle had built a vaginal suppository specifically for women like me. Hyaluronic acid for hydration. Lactobacillus lactis for the bacterial balance. Glycogen as the food source for those bacteria. And polydextrose as the prebiotic fiber that keeps the colony fed between doses.

I read every ingredient out loud at my kitchen table the way I used to read lab values.

Hyaluronic acid. Lactobacillus lactis. Glycogen. Polydextrose.

None of those 4 molecules is on the no-list my oncologist had given me. Not one.

Hyaluronic acid is a sugar molecule that holds water. It does not bind to the estrogen receptor. Lactobacillus lactis is a bacterium. It is not a hormone. Glycogen is a carbohydrate, the same one your liver stores energy in. Polydextrose is a food-grade soluble fiber.

No estrogen. No phytoestrogens. No DHEA. No hormone analogs. No parabens. No phthalates.

The exact ingredient list a survivor like me had been told for 2 years did not exist.

I printed the product information and brought it to my next oncology appointment along with the ASCO guideline. My oncologist read both pages while I sat on the exam table in a paper gown.

She looked up at me and said, "I have no objection to this."

That was the most important sentence she had said to me in 2 years.

Reviewed, not approved. No objection, not endorsement. That is the language an evidence-based decision actually sounds like when the patient walks into the room with the evidence in her hand.

I started Avelle the next week.

The first month, the burning was gone. Not reduced. Gone.

The second month, the dryness lifted in a way it had not lifted on Replens, on coconut oil, on any of the lubricants the oncology office had handed me.

By the third month, my husband took my hand on the couch one Sunday afternoon and I did not flinch.

That was the first time in 19 months.

If you are on letrozole or anastrozole or exemestane, and your oncologist has handed you a tube of something with the energy of a parting gift, this is what I want you to know.

The first-line treatment for what is happening to you is not lube. It is not Replens. It is not coconut oil.

The guidelines, the actual guidelines your oncologist trained on, say it is a non-hormonal vaginal moisturizer used regularly.

The category is real. There is a product that meets the modern definition of what those words actually mean.

You are allowed to want your body back. You are not betraying your survivorship by asking for relief. You are not asking for hormones.

You are asking for what the guidelines explicitly endorsed 7 years ago and somehow nobody has bothered to deliver to you in a form that actually works.

When I went to the order page, I noticed the small print at the bottom. Reviewed by oncologists. Per-lot third-party testing. A printable handout you could bring to your next appointment so your oncologist could read it the way mine did and say whether she had any objection.

3 things I had not seen on a single product anyone in oncology had ever recommended to me.

Now I want to say the part I was most afraid to say when I first started writing this.

There are 2 kinds of women who finish reading this letter. There is no third kind.

The first kind closes the tab. She tells herself she will think about it. She tells herself the burning is probably going to ease on its own. She goes back to the Replens, or she goes back to nothing, and 6 months from now she is in the same exam room, in the same paper gown, having the same 3-minute conversation with the same tired PA.

The polite version of the standard of care is the only version she ever gets, because she never asked for the other one.

The second kind prints the handout. She brings it to the next visit. She watches her oncologist read it. She listens for the sentence "I have no objection." And then she finds out, over the next 3 or 4 months, what her body actually does when it is given the 4 things the guideline has been pointing at since 2018.

The actual risk, the one I want you to feel in your stomach the way I felt it the morning I read "undetectable," is not the box.

The risk is the next 18 months looking exactly like the last 18 months. The risk is your husband stopping reaching first, or you stopping responding first, and neither of you remembering the order anymore. The risk is the slow erosion of the small everyday touch that a long marriage is actually built out of.

None of that goes on a chart. None of that gets billed.

But it is the real cost of the polite version, and it compounds.

The wasted thing is not the box. The wasted thing is the months you keep waiting for your body to come back on its own.

It will not.

Mine didn't either, until I asked for the actual standard.

When I went to order, I noticed they had a 90-day money-back guarantee printed right on the page.

I sat with that for a minute.

I had spent 30 years inside hospital administration and I had never, in 3 decades, watched a pharmaceutical manufacturer offer a patient her money back if the drug did not work. Not once.

The Replens did not come with a refund offer. The coconut oil did not. The lubricants the PA had recommended did not.

The first time anyone in 2 years of survivorship had said, in writing, that if their product did not do what it claimed I would get my money back, was a small company I had found through a clinical trial registry.

That alone shifted something for me.

I had read enough by that point to understand why they made the batches small. Lactobacillus lactis is a live culture, and the glycogen it feeds on has a finite shelf-active window once the suppository is formed. They batch-produce because they will not ship a bottle whose colony has aged out of viability sitting in a warehouse.

The trade-off is that they sell out for a few weeks at a stretch.

If they are in stock the day you click through, that is the day to order. You do not wait until next week.

If you are reading this at 6 in the morning the way I read my chart at 6 in the morning, you already know which of the 2 kinds of women you are.

The one who closes the tab and goes back to Replens for another 18 months. Or the one who prints the handout, brings it to the appointment, and finds out what "I have no objection" sounds like in her own oncologist's voice.

The husband on the couch is still reaching.

The question is whether you are still flinching 19 months from now.
creative.title: The Word On My Lab Was "Undetectable." That Was The Day I Started Reading.
